title: The library that was lost
hook: the Sikh Reference Library, with old handwritten manuscripts, was lost in the operation's aftermath

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghallughara: the army in the Harmandir complex on a holy day, the Akal Takht damaged. Remember the pilgrims. Today, a quieter loss from the same days, made of paper and ink.

A letter from a great-grandparent. A wedding photograph gone brown at the edges. A recipe written in a hand nobody alive can match. If a fire took them, no shop could sell them back. Now widen that to a whole people: the handwriting of their history, some of it centuries old, kept in one building. That building stood inside the Harmandir complex until June 1984.
screen: `A LETTER, A PHOTOGRAPH, A RECIPE.` → `NO SHOP SELLS IT BACK.` → `A WHOLE BUILDING OF THEM.`

segments.voice: It was called the Sikh Reference Library, set up in the complex in the 1940s. What was in it? Handwritten copies of the Guru Granth Sahib, some very old, copied out by hand long before printing. Hukamnamas: letters of instruction to Sikh communities, some said to have been sent by the Gurus themselves. Rare books, old histories, documents of the Singh Sabha and the gurdwara reform movement. Scholars came from far away to read there. It was the community's memory, on shelves. In June 1984, the library burned. How it happened is disputed. The army's account says it caught fire during the fighting. Many Sikhs, and some witnesses, say the fighting had ended first, that the building was burned afterward, and that boxes of material were carried away before the fire. Over the years, some items have been returned. Many have never been found. Sikh bodies still ask for the rest to be given back, and the question is still open. Why does a library matter so much, in a week when people died? Because the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru, and handwritten copies carried the Guru's word across generations. A hukamnama in a Guru's hand is a thread straight back to them. Losing them is like losing the family letters, except the family is a whole community. Memory, here, is not just knowledge. It is connection.
screen: `THE SIKH REFERENCE LIBRARY.` · `HANDWRITTEN GRANTHS AND HUKAMNAMAS.` · `IT BURNED; HOW IS DISPUTED.` · `THE GURU'S WORD, CARRIED BY HAND.` · then, large: `MEMORY IS PRECIOUS.`

segments.voice: If you can, hold something old: a book, a photograph, a letter, anything that carries someone's memory; if nothing is nearby, picture one. Look at it slowly, the paper, the handwriting, the wear at the corners, and think of who made it and who kept it safe so it could reach you. Let yourself be grateful to the keepers.
Hukamnama. A letter of command from the Gurus — among the handwritten Granths and hukamnamas lost when the Sikh Reference Library burned after June 1984.
Your line: memory is precious. Some of it is still waiting to come home. Day three hundred nine, kept.

howItsDone: Sikh institutions continue to ask for the return of manuscripts and documents from the Sikh Reference Library, and Sikhs remember its loss as part of the June remembrance each year.
